title: Why Is Being Busy a Status Symbol? The Psychology Behind Hustle Culture
subtitle: Being busy became a status symbol because, in many modern economies, time is the scarcest thing a person owns, and a full calendar signals that someone else values it. Research on "conspicuous consumption of time" found that people who appear busy are judged as more competent, ambitious and in demand. It is a signal, and signals can be faked, which is why the habit outlives its usefulness.
author: Avani Jain
key_takeaways: The old status symbol was leisure. The new one is scarcity: "I am the scarce resource, so I am valuable."
This is not universal. In a well-known study, Americans read busyness as high status while Italians read long hours as low status.
Busyness is easy to perform and hard to verify, so it becomes a competition in display rather than output.
The costs are measurable: WHO and ILO data link 55-plus hour weeks to higher risks of stroke and heart disease, and Gallup finds global employee engagement at just 21%.
Most of the research is Western. Whether India follows the American or the Italian pattern is an open question, and this article treats it as one.
content:
What does it mean to say busyness is a status symbol?

Ask someone how they are and count how many say "busy" before "fine". The word has become a polite boast. It carries a small payload of information: I am in demand, I am useful, someone is waiting for me.

A status symbol is anything that tells strangers where you sit in a pecking order without you having to say so. A watch does this. A school name does this. Increasingly, a full diary does this too, which is odd, because for most of recorded history the person with an empty diary was the one in charge.

How did we get here from the leisure class?

In 1899 the economist Thorstein Veblen described the "leisure class": people whose status was proven by not having to work, and by consuming conspicuously to show it. Idleness was the trophy.

Then something flipped. In 2017, Silvia Bellezza, Neeru Paharia and Anat Keinan published a paper in the Journal of Consumer Research arguing that busyness has become a new form of conspicuous consumption. In their experiments, a busy person was seen as more competent and ambitious, and as a scarcer commodity in the labour market. In one experiment with 100 participants, the busy character scored 5.44 on a seven-point status scale against 2.55 for the leisurely one.

Keinan put the logic in one line: the new conspicuous consumption is about saying, "I am the scarce resource, and therefore I am valuable."

The mechanism is old and simple. We admire what is scarce. When goods became cheap, scarcity migrated to the one asset money cannot manufacture: attention and hours.

Is this true everywhere, or only in some places?

Not everywhere, and this is where the story gets interesting.

Place studied How busyness was read Why researchers think so
United States Long hours and scarce leisure signalled higher status Strong belief that effort and ambition drive social mobility
Italy Long hours were associated with lower status Status historically tied to inherited standing and leisure

Source: Bellezza, Paharia and Keinan (2017), as summarised by Harvard Business School.

The authors point to perceived social mobility. Where people believe effort can move them up, a visible display of effort reads as proof of climbing. Where status is inherited or fixed, a busy person looks like someone who has to work for a living.

This matters for anyone selling, hiring or writing in more than one market. "Hustle" is not a universal virtue. It is a local story about how people rise.

What about India?

Here we have to be honest: the large, controlled studies have not been done at scale. What exists is public conversation. In 2023, Infosys co-founder N. R. Narayana Murthy suggested young Indians should be prepared to work 70 hours a week, and the debate that followed was less about the number than about the story behind it. Supporters read it as a country in a hurry. Critics read it as a demand for sacrifice with no promise of mobility attached.

One commentator writing in ThePrint pointed out that India's 2019-20 time-use survey showed urban working men aged 20 to 29 spending about 8.5 hours a day at work, and women of the same age about 6.5 hours at work plus nearly three hours on domestic work, leaving roughly an hour and twenty minutes of leisure. That is not the picture of a workforce short on effort.

A hypothesis, flagged as one: in a country where aspiration is strong and mobility is believed in but unevenly delivered, busyness may work as both a status marker and a hedge. Looking tired and occupied is proof you are in the race. Nobody has measured this properly, so treat it as a question worth asking, not a finding.

Why is busyness so easy to fake?

Because it is a signal about input, not output. A calendar full of calls, a message sent at 11:40 pm, a "quick sync" that lasts an hour: all of these are visible. The thing they supposedly prove, valuable work done, is invisible and slow.

When a signal is cheap to produce and hard to check, two things happen. First, people produce more of it. Second, the signal gets worse at telling you anything. This is why a meeting-heavy day can feel exhausting and still leave nothing finished.

What does it cost?

The costs show up in the data, not just in the mood.

  • Health. A WHO and ILO study estimated that long working hours were linked to 745,000 deaths from stroke and ischaemic heart disease in 2016. Working 55 or more hours a week was associated with a 35 percent higher risk of stroke and a 17 percent higher risk of dying from heart disease, compared with 35 to 40 hours. The burden was highest in the Western Pacific and South-East Asia regions.
  • Engagement. Gallup's 2025 report put global employee engagement at 21 percent, down two points, with an estimated US$438 billion in lost productivity. For the South Asia region it found the lowest share of people "thriving" anywhere in the world, at 15 percent.
  • Judgement. Busy people make more time for meetings and less for the thinking that makes meetings worth having.

Correlation is not causation, and these studies cannot tell you which hours did the damage. They do tell you that the trade is real.

What should we notice instead?

  • Ask what the busyness is buying. If the answer is respect, there may be cheaper ways to earn it.
  • Count output where you can. A team that can say what it finished this week is less likely to compete on how late it stayed.
  • Watch the language. "Slammed" and "swamped" are mostly status words dressed as complaints. Try replying with what you are working on and why it matters.
  • Notice who gets to be unbusy. In many places, the people with the most power are now the ones who protect their time most visibly. The old leisure-class signal has not disappeared. It has gone quiet.
  • Notice the market you are in. If you advertise "hustle" to an audience that reads effort as low status, the message will land backwards.

Frequently asked questions

Why is being busy considered a status symbol?

Because time has become scarce, and scarce things signal value. Research on conspicuous consumption of time found that busy people are judged as more competent, ambitious and in demand, especially where people believe effort leads to social mobility.

Is hustle culture the same in every country?

No. A widely cited study found Americans read busyness as high status while Italians read long working hours as lower status. Culture, perceived social mobility and history shape how effort is judged.

Is working long hours bad for your health?

Evidence says it can be. A WHO and ILO analysis linked working 55 or more hours a week to a 35 percent higher risk of stroke and a 17 percent higher risk of dying from ischaemic heart disease than a 35 to 40 hour week.

Does being busy mean being productive?

Not necessarily. Busyness measures visible effort, while productivity measures output. Gallup's 2025 data shows global engagement at 21 percent, which suggests long hours alone do not translate into committed, effective work.

Sources

  • Harvard Business School Working Knowledge, "Having No Life Is the New Aspirational Lifestyle". https://www.library.hbs.edu/working-knowledge/having-no-life-is-the-new-aspirational-lifestyle
  • WHO and ILO, "Long working hours increasing deaths from heart disease and stroke" (17 May 2021), via PAHO. https://www.paho.org/en/news/17-5-2021-long-working-hours-increasing-deaths-heart-disease-and-stroke-who-ilo
  • Gallup, State of the Global Workplace 2025. https://gallup.com/file/workplace/659528/state-of-the-global-workplace-2025-download.pdf
  • ThePrint, "What Indians got wrong about the 70-hour work debate". https://theprint.in/opinion/what-indians-got-wrong-about-the-70-hour-work-debate/1936389/

title: Why Do Superstitions Survive? What Folk Beliefs Reveal About Culture and Human Behaviour
subtitle: Superstitions survive because they do jobs that facts do not: they reduce anxiety when outcomes are uncertain, give people a feeling of control, and bind a community through shared ritual. They also cost very little to keep. The belief rarely needs to be true. It only needs to be useful, familiar and cheap enough to repeat.
author: Avani Jain
key_takeaways: Superstition tends to appear where uncertainty is high and control is low, a pattern the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski saw in Trobriand fishing.
Believing in luck can change performance, probably by raising confidence, not by changing luck.
Folk beliefs are also social glue, and some become self-fulfilling at population scale, as Japan's 1966 "Fire Horse" year showed.
Many headline claims about superstition are contested. The "number four kills" cardiac study, for one, failed to replicate in Hong Kong.
A superstition is a useful map of what a community fears, wants and cannot control.
content:
Why are people still superstitious?

You would think the habit would have died out. We have weather satellites, clinical trials and a search engine in every pocket. Yet in a 1996 Gallup poll, 25 percent of Americans said they were "very" or "somewhat" superstitious, up from 18 percent in 1990. A 2022 YouGov poll of 1,000 US adults found that 12 percent always or frequently carry or wear a lucky charm and another 19 percent do so occasionally or rarely.

Superstition is not a leftover from a less educated age. It is a feature of how minds cope with uncertainty, and uncertainty has not gone anywhere.

What do superstitions actually do for us?

Three things, and each is worth taking seriously.

1. They calm us down when we cannot control the outcome. In the 1910s, Malinowski studied fishing in the Trobriand Islands. Fishing in the safe lagoon involved no magic. Fishing in the dangerous open sea came wrapped in extensive ritual for safety and success. His reading: ritual rises with danger and unpredictability. The more you cannot control, the more you reach for something you can do.

2. They can change how we perform. Damisch, Stoberock and Mussweiler (2010) ran four experiments on the effect of good-luck superstitions. In one, participants who were told the golf ball was lucky sank 6.42 putts out of 10, against 4.75 in the control group. The researchers' explanation is not magic but self-efficacy: a lucky charm raises confidence, which raises persistence, which raises results. The samples were small (28 to 51 students per experiment), so read this as suggestive, not settled.

3. They hold groups together. A ritual done by many people is a shared language. When you hang something on a door because everyone does, you are saying you belong here.

Are superstitions just accidents of learning?

Partly. In 1948 the psychologist B. F. Skinner fed pigeons at random intervals. According to a summary of his work, six of the eight birds developed repeated behaviours such as spinning, rocking and head jerking, as if the action had caused the food. His point was that animals, and by extension people, link whatever they were doing to whatever happened next.

That is a useful idea, and it explains why a lucky shirt feels lucky after one good day. But the study was small, and its interpretation has been argued over for decades. It explains how a personal habit forms. It does not explain why millions of people share the same one.

Do rituals create fear, or soothe it?

This is the best argument in the field, and both sides have a point.

Malinowski said anxiety comes first and ritual is the response. His rival Radcliffe-Brown said it works the other way: it is unlikely an Andaman Islander would think eating certain foods was dangerous if not for the ritual that says so. In other words, the rule creates the fear.

Most scholars today lean towards both being true. People feel real anxiety, and societies shape which anxieties are worth having and which rituals answer them.

How do shared beliefs reshape a whole society?

Sometimes a folk belief gets big enough to show up in the national statistics.

In Japan, the zodiac year of the Fire Horse (hinoeuma) is believed to produce daughters with fiery tempers who shorten their husbands' lives. The belief traces to a 1662 poetry collection. In 1966, a Fire Horse year, Japan recorded just 1,360,974 births, a fall of about 25 percent from the year before. Arranged marriages were roughly half of all marriages at the time, which made a zodiac "flaw" a matchmaking liability and gave the belief teeth.

The next Fire Horse year came in 2026. Commentary at the start of the year noted far fewer arranged marriages and a much lower fear factor among prospective parents. The belief did not need to be disproved. The institutions that enforced it simply weakened.

That is the lesson for anyone who works with culture: a superstition survives as long as the systems that carry it do.

Which famous superstition claims should we be careful with?

Several. A 2001 study by David Phillips and colleagues reported that cardiac deaths among Chinese and Japanese Americans peaked on the fourth of the month, 13 percent above expectation overall and 27 percent in California. The number four sounds like "death" in Chinese and Japanese, so the finding made headlines.

It has been challenged since. A critique reported that the original study used only 5 of 36 heart disease codes and, in the remaining 31, found no excess of deaths on day four. A Hong Kong study covering 1995 to 2000 found no effect on the fourth, fourteenth or twenty-fourth of the month, despite a heavily Cantonese-speaking, strongly superstitious population.

The honest position: the idea that belief can affect health is plausible and worth studying, and this specific result is shaky.

What does a local superstition tell you about a place?

A good deal. Take nimbu mirchi, the string of seven chillies and one lemon hung outside shops and homes across India. The traditional explanation is that Alakshmi, the goddess of poverty and misfortune, is drawn to sour and spicy tastes, so the offering keeps her at the threshold and out of the business. The same bundle sits at the front of a stall in Delhi's Chandni Chowk.

Read as a data point, it tells you who is anxious about what. A small trader hanging protection above the till is expressing a real fear about luck and cash flow in a business where margins are thin and the weather, the supplier and the customer are all out of his control. This is Malinowski's open sea, with a billing counter.

For brands, the practical reading is respect. Nobody needs a campaign explaining why the lemon is wrong. People need products and services that understand the uncertainty the lemon is answering.

What should marketers and builders take from this?

  • Look for the anxiety behind the ritual. If a belief is stable, something uncontrollable sits behind it.
  • Do not mock, and do not exploit. Fear is a strong lever and a poor foundation.
  • Check how the belief is enforced. Institutions, families and marketplaces keep rituals alive. When they change, behaviour follows, as Japan showed.
  • Treat headline stats with suspicion. The most quoted superstition findings are often the least replicated.
  • Remember the sample. One village, one family or one shop is a clue, not a culture.

Frequently asked questions

Why do people believe in superstitions?

Because superstitions reduce anxiety and create a feeling of control in uncertain situations. Studies suggest they can also raise confidence and persistence, which may improve performance, and shared rituals strengthen belonging within a community.

Do superstitions actually work?

Not by changing luck. A 2010 set of experiments found that people with a lucky charm performed better on tasks like golf putting, likely because confidence and persistence rose. The samples were small, so the findings are suggestive rather than definitive.

How many people are superstitious?

It depends on how it is asked. A 1996 Gallup poll found 25 percent of Americans called themselves very or somewhat superstitious, and a 2022 YouGov poll found about 31 percent carry or wear a lucky charm at least occasionally.

What is the nimbu mirchi superstition?

It is a string of seven chillies and one lemon hung outside shops and homes in India. It is traditionally said to appease Alakshmi, the goddess of misfortune, so she stays outside and keeps bad luck away from the premises.

  • YouGov, "Which superstitions are Americans most likely to believe?" (April 2022). https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/42425-which-superstitions-are-americans-most-likely-beli
  • Damisch, Stoberock and Mussweiler, "Keep Your Fingers Crossed! How Superstition Improves Performance", Psychological Science 21(7), 2010. https://www.hf.uni-koeln.de/data/dppsenglich/File/PDFSStudien/PsychS21_7.pdf
  • Association for Psychological Science, "Silly Sports Rituals? Think Again". https://www.psychologicalscience.org/publications/observer/obsonline/silly-sports-rituals-think-again.html
  • Critique summary of Skinner (1948), "Superstition in the Pigeon". https://communities.pacificu.edu/arhevaninetti/?p=177

title: Why Consumers Trust Brands Less in the Age of AI, and What Marketers Should Notice
subtitle: Consumers trust brands less in the age of AI because AI has made content cheap to produce and hard to verify. Surveys in 2026 find that roughly a third to more than half of consumers say visible AI use lowers their trust or their willingness to buy, depending on how the question is asked. The penalty is rarely about the technology. It is about the suspected absence of a person who stands behind the work.
author: Avani Jain
key_takeaways: Trust drops when AI use is visible, undisclosed or misleading, not simply when AI is used.
In one UK study, people engaged less with identical content once they were told AI had made it.
Effort used to prove care. When effort costs nothing, brands need new proof: a named person, a specific point of view, a consequence for being wrong.
Most of the data comes from the US and UK, and several surveys are published by companies that sell content tools. Read the numbers as direction, not law.
content:
What does the 2026 data say about AI and brand trust?

Start with the numbers, then argue with them.

Source (date) Who was asked What it found
YouGov (April 2026) Consumers across several markets 32% would trust a brand less if its content was made with AI; 15% would trust it more
Fractl (Q2 2026) 1,008 consumers and 150 marketers Share saying heavy AI use would lower trust in a favourite brand rose from 20% to about 40%; only 14% would trust a brand more
Optimizely (September 2026) 1,000 UK consumers and 100 marketers 62% trust marketing content less since brands began using AI; 66% think brands favour volume over quality
Clutch (August 2026) 601 US consumers 53% are less likely to buy from brands they know use AI in social content; nearly 90% want AI content disclosed
Capgemini (2023 to 2025) Global consumer tracking Trust in AI-generated content fell from 73% to 55% in two years, across every age group

The percentages differ because the questions differ. The direction does not. Different samples, different wording, same slope.

Why does the same content feel different once people know AI made it?

Bynder's survey of 2,000 UK consumers found that people often preferred AI-generated content when it was unlabelled, then 52% felt less engaged once they were told AI had made the same thing. Same words. Same pictures. Different feeling.

That is the most interesting number in this article, because it moves the problem. The content did not get worse. The meaning of the content changed.

Economists call this costly signalling. A handwritten note says more than a printed one, not because the handwriting is better, but because it cost someone an evening. For most of marketing's history, effort was a rough proxy for care. A beautifully produced film told you a brand had money and commitment. A thoughtful reply told you someone was listening. Generative AI cut the price of polish to nearly zero, and a signal that costs nothing stops signalling anything.

What fills the gap is proof that a particular human stands behind the work: a name, a strong opinion, specificity nobody could have guessed, a consequence if the brand is wrong.

Is the problem AI itself, or what brands do with it?

The data points to the second. YouGov found that trust falls sharply when AI content feels misleading, goes undisclosed, or replaces human creativity entirely. Clutch found that 64% would trust a brand or creator less if AI misrepresented a product, while 42% viewed AI positively for educational content. Optimizely found that 67% find AI-generated images of people in ads creepy, and that 72% are more likely to engage with content that feels human rather than automated.

Read together, people do not object to a tool. They object to a counterfeit. AI as an instrument (a researcher, an editor, a translator) rarely triggers the reaction. AI as the invisible author, speaking in a human voice, does.

Does this hold in every market and generation?

Not evenly. Bynder found that 71% of people aged 55 and over want AI content disclosed, against 45% of 16 to 24 year olds. Younger audiences are less insistent on labels. That is not the same as being less sceptical, and Capgemini's trend line fell across every age group, Gen Z included.

Geography is the bigger gap, and it is worth being honest about. Almost all of the 2026 data we found was collected in the US and UK. In markets where trust travels through people (the shopkeeper, the family WhatsApp group, the creator you have followed for years), the penalty for "no human behind this" may be steeper. It may also be the opposite. Nobody has measured it at scale. Treat any confident claim about India or Southeast Asia as a hypothesis, including ours.

What should marketers actually notice?

  • Attitudes are not behaviour. These are stated preferences. Clutch found that 86% of respondents had already encountered AI-generated content on social media, and plenty of people who say they distrust it still click on it. Track what people do, not only what they tell surveys.
  • Check who paid for the survey. Several of the studies above come from firms that sell content platforms or marketing services. That does not make them wrong. It makes them interested.
  • The trust tax is paid on suspicion, not proof. 57% of UK consumers told Optimizely they can usually tell when content is AI-made. Confidence is not accuracy, but belief is what drives the reaction. If audiences think your content is machine-made, it behaves as if it is.
  • Spend the saved time on specificity. The hours AI gives back should go into what it cannot fake: first-hand observation, local context, a position you would defend in public.
  • Treat disclosure as design, not compliance. Between 84% and 91% of consumers in Fractl's survey wanted AI content labelled, depending on format. Decide what you will disclose, where, and in what tone before a customer decides for you. Rules on disclosure vary by country, so check yours.

What does trust-first use of AI look like in practice?

Two brands use AI to draft product pages. One publishes the draft. The other has a named editor rewrite it with something only a person at that company would know (a supplier detail, a customer complaint, a known flaw) and signs it.

Same tool. Different promise. The second brand is not using less AI. It is putting a person's reputation behind the output. That, not the absence of AI, is what audiences are asking for.

Trust used to be a by-product of effort. Now it is a decision, made page by page, by someone willing to put their name on it.

Frequently asked questions

Do consumers trust AI-generated content?

Mostly with caution. In 2026 surveys, between roughly a third and more than half of consumers say they would trust a brand less, or buy less, once they know AI made its content. Trust is lowest when AI use is hidden, misleading or replaces human creativity entirely.

Should brands disclose when they use AI?

Consumer expectation points that way. Fractl found that 84% to 91% want AI content labelled, depending on format, and Clutch found that nearly 90% expect disclosure on social media. Legal requirements differ by country, so check local rules, then decide your disclosure approach deliberately.

Does using AI hurt brand trust?

It can, mainly when use is undisclosed, misleading or a substitute for human creativity. YouGov's 2026 data shows 32% would trust a brand less for AI-made content against 15% who would trust it more, so the effect is real but not universal.

How can marketers use AI without losing trust?

Use it as an instrument, not an invisible author. Keep a named human accountable for every published piece, add specifics only your team could know, disclose in plain language where audiences expect it, and measure behaviour as well as survey sentiment.

Sources

  • Search Engine Land and Fractl, AI search adoption and consumer trust study (2026). https://searchengineland.com/ai-search-adoption-rises-consumer-trust-declines-study-480338
  • ContentGrip, summary of the Fractl Q2 2026 survey. https://www.contentgrip.com/ai-trust-search-2026/
  • Optimizely, "Six in 10 consumers say AI has made brand marketing less trustworthy" (22 September 2026). https://www.optimizely.com/company/press/ai-trustworthiness-uk/
  • Clutch, "53% of Consumers Are Less Likely to Buy From Brands Using AI on Social Media" (8 September 2026). https://clutch.co/press-releases/ai-social-media-report
  • MarTech, "Consumers like AI content until they know it's AI" (Bynder and Capgemini data). https://martech.org/consumers-like-ai-content-until-they-know-its-ai/

title: Why Do Canadians Drink Cold Beverages in Winter? A Lesson in Consumer Context
subtitle: Many Canadians drink cold beverages in winter because temperature is not the rule they decide by. Heated homes, cars and underground walkways mean cold is something you cross between warm rooms, not something you live inside, so drink choices follow habit and occasion. The clearest evidence is iced coffee: a trade report says Tim Hortons' iced drinks kept selling through a December 2025 cold snap in Ontario.
author: Avani Jain
key_takeaways: The claim worth testing is not that Canadians crave cold drinks in winter. It is that winter does not forbid them.
In India, Ayurvedic seasonal guidance (ritucharya) advises against cold drinks in winter, which turns a drink choice into a seasonal rule. Canada has no equivalent rule.
Canadian cities have spent decades engineering winter out of daily routine. Toronto's PATH runs about 30 kilometres and Montreal's RÉSO about 32.
One shop on one night is a sample of one. It is how you find a question, not how you answer it.
content:
What did I see in that Ontario convenience store?

Christmas Eve, 2017. I had been in Canada a few weeks. Late evening, a small convenience store in London, Ontario, snow outside. People came in, walked past the hot coffee, and picked up cold soft drinks from a chiller, bottles of what they called pop. Nobody hesitated. Nobody made a face about the weather. I had grown up in a place where a cold drink in winter earns a raised eyebrow, and I stood there like an anthropologist who had forgotten her notebook.

Then there was the word. "Pop" is the dominant term for a fizzy drink across most of Canada, while "soda," the favourite of the American northeast and southwest, has virtually no currency there, according to the UBC-hosted Dictionary of Canadianisms on Historical Principles, which draws on the work of linguist Charles Boberg. My read: a word like pop files the drink under everyday treat, not under refreshment for hot weather. I did not have that filing system yet.

Do Canadians really drink more cold drinks in winter?

Nobody has shown that, and we found no data that says so. Canadians almost certainly drink fewer cold drinks in January than in July. What I saw was not appetite. It was the absence of a prohibition.

That distinction decides everything. "Why do they crave cold drinks in the cold?" is a question with a false premise. "Why does winter not forbid cold drinks there?" is the one worth answering.

The evidence that winter does not forbid them is better than one night in one shop. Tim Hortons launched the Iced Capp in 1999 and still describes it as a summertime favourite. Yet a World Coffee Portal report on Restaurant Brands International's results said Canadians kept lining up for the chain's iced drinks through December 2025, with Ontario averaging about minus 9 degrees Celsius in what the report called the harshest cold snap in fifty years. A Canadian student newspaper column even treats ordering an Iced Capp in extreme cold as a small credential of Canadian-ness. The behaviour has been promoted from allowed to a bit of a badge.

What rulebook was I carrying?

In India, winter eating has a rulebook, and it is old. Ayurveda's ritucharya, the seasonal regimen, divides the year into six seasons and attaches a way of eating to each. For Hemanta, the early-winter season running roughly from mid-November to mid-January, published Ayurvedic guidance advises warm, nourishing food and avoiding cold drinks and refrigerated meals, on the logic that winter strengthens digestion and cold drinks undermine it.

Hardly anyone in an Indian household cites the text. The rule travels as folk advice: do not have cold things now, you will catch a cold. Whether that holds up medically is a separate question, and not one this article tries to settle. As a behavioural rule it is powerful either way. It passes across the dinner table and works without anyone remembering where it came from.

So what I would have called discipline back home is closer to compliance, with a rule I had absorbed so completely I could not see it was a rule.

What rulebook was the Canadian shopper carrying?

Probably none about temperature, and that is the point. Canada did not build a seasonal dietary code. It built infrastructure. Toronto's PATH links more than 70 buildings through roughly 30 kilometres of tunnels and walkways. Montreal's RÉSO, at about 32 kilometres, took the Guinness record for the world's largest underground network from Toronto in 2023. Add heated homes, heated cars and heated malls.

The effect is that cold becomes something you cross between warm rooms rather than something you live inside. When your body rarely sits in sustained cold, the temperature of a drink stops being a question about your body. It becomes a question about taste, habit and occasion.

Occasion is my second hypothesis, and I would label it that way. It was Christmas Eve. Pop at a holiday is closer to a treat than a thirst-quencher, the way eggnog or shortbread is. I cannot prove that from one night. It is what I would test first.

India, in winter Ontario, in winter
What the rule says Seasonal guidance advises against cold drinks No seasonal rule about cold drinks
Where it lives Folk advice passed between family members Infrastructure: heated homes, cars and walkways
What decides the drink Season and the body Habit, taste and occasion

What should marketers take from this?

  • Climate is not context. The weather outside is not the environment people live in. Engineered environments can make a place's climate irrelevant to its habits.
  • Find the rulebook before judging the behaviour. Every consumer carries one, usually invisible to them. Your job is to find it, and to notice when yours is not theirs.
  • Occasion can outrank season. If a brand's calendar assumes weather drives demand, test whether it does. Iced drinks selling in a Canadian winter is a reminder that seasonal assumptions are often inherited, not measured.
  • Cultural permission can become identity. When defying the weather becomes a marker of belonging, a product has not just been allowed, it has been adopted. That is a far stronger position than tolerance.
  • A sample of one is a question, not a finding. Check monthly sales by region, talk to locals, and compare with a second city before building a plan on a hunch.

I went to Canada thinking I was watching a lack of restraint. I left with a better question: whose rules am I applying? Every market has a rulebook. Most of the work is learning which one you are standing in.

Frequently asked questions

Do Canadians drink cold drinks in winter?

Many do. A World Coffee Portal report on Restaurant Brands International's results said Tim Hortons' iced drinks sold strongly through a December 2025 cold snap in Ontario. We found no data comparing winter and summer consumption, so the safe claim is that winter does not stop Canadians from drinking cold drinks, not that they drink more.

Why do Canadians call soda pop?

"Pop" is the dominant word for a carbonated soft drink across most of Canada, while "soda" has virtually no currency there, according to the Dictionary of Canadianisms on Historical Principles. Pockets such as Montreal and parts of eastern Ontario lean towards "soft drink".

What does Ayurveda say about cold drinks in winter?

Ayurveda's seasonal regimen, ritucharya, advises warm, nourishing food in winter and avoiding cold drinks and refrigerated meals, on the principle that they weaken digestion. It is a traditional guideline, not a medical finding.

What is consumer context?

Consumer context is the set of physical, cultural and social conditions that shape why people buy or behave as they do: climate, infrastructure, habit, belief and occasion. The same product can mean very different things in different contexts.

title: Why Human Behaviour Cannot Be Explained by Data Alone: Culture, History and Economics Matter Too
subtitle: Data tells you what people did. It cannot tell you why, because the why lives in things most datasets do not capture: culture (what a group treats as normal), history (what a place has already decided) and economics (what people can afford to choose). Without them, behavioural data produces accurate descriptions and wrong explanations.
author: Avani Jain
key_takeaways: The same data point can come from very different causes, and the number cannot say which.
Nokia's numbers were huge and still missed what an ethnographer saw on the street.

Much of what we call human nature was measured on a narrow slice of the world: 96% of subjects in a 2008 survey of top psychology journals came from Western industrialised countries, which hold about 12% of the population.
A better method reads history first, lived perception second and data third, and says how sure it is.
content:
Why does data describe behaviour so well and explain it so badly?

Data is a witness. It reports faithfully on what happened: who clicked, who left, who paid. It is a poor judge of why. The reason is structural. Behaviour is the visible end of a chain that begins in belief, history and money, and data usually captures only the last link.

Take a falling conversion rate in one city. It could mean the price is wrong. It could mean the product contradicts a local custom. It could mean a festival, a rumour, a rival's launch or a regulator. The number is identical in every case. If you treat the number as the explanation, you will fix the wrong thing very efficiently.

What did Nokia's numbers miss?

In 2009, ethnographer Tricia Wang was working for Nokia, researching how low-income people in China used phones. Living among migrants and street vendors, she concluded they were ready to pay for pricier smartphones than the industry assumed. Nokia's response, as she has told it, was that her sample of about a hundred people looked weak beside several million data points. Her lesson, widely quoted since: "What is measurable isn't the same as what is valuable."

A caution about the story. Nokia's handset business was later sold to Microsoft, and the tale is often told as simple cause and effect. The real causality is tangled. The lesson does not depend on it. The big dataset was tidy, enormous and silent about what a street vendor in China wanted. Wang calls the missing ingredient thick data: qualitative insight into people's emotions, stories and models of their world. Her argument is not that big data is wrong, but that businesses need both.

Whose behaviour is the data actually about?

Datasets are not neutral samples of humanity. In 2010, Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan pointed out that a 2008 survey of top psychology journals found 96% of subjects came from Western industrialised countries, which house about 12% of the world's population. They coined the acronym WEIRD (Western, educated, industrialised, rich, democratic) and argued that on a range of measures such people are outliers, not the human default.

Marketing inherits the same bias in a different costume. A panel built from urban smartphone owners describes urban smartphone owners. A survey in English describes people who answer surveys in English. When a finding about "consumers" turns out to be about a particular slice of them, the problem is not accuracy. It is the question: whose behaviour is this a record of?

Can the same numbers point to opposite conclusions?

Yes, and the textbook case is almost embarrassingly clean. In 1973, the University of California, Berkeley received 12,763 complete graduate applications. About 44% of men were admitted against 35% of women, a gap large enough to invite a sex-discrimination suit. Statisticians Peter Bickel, Eugene Hammel and William O'Connell then looked department by department. The gap largely vanished, and in several departments it reversed. Women had applied more often to the most competitive departments, where almost everyone was rejected. Their 1975 paper in Science became the classic example of Simpson's paradox.

The statistics explain the reversal. They do not explain why applicants sorted themselves that way. That question belongs to schooling, expectation, culture and history, none of which is in the spreadsheet. Data raised the question. Context was always going to have to answer it.

What can history explain that a dashboard cannot?

In June 2026, the Khasi Hills Autonomous District Council in Meghalaya refused the quick-commerce platform Blinkit a trading licence, citing the risk to more than 4,000 local grocery shops. Blinkit had begun operating in Shillong and engaged hundreds of delivery partners before halting services. The council's chief executive member said it had earlier refused licences to similar ventures, including Instamart. The licensing system the council administers rests on a regulation from 1954 governing trading by non-tribals, written for a world with no delivery apps.

A dashboard of Shillong orders would have shown healthy growth right up to the day it showed zero. The signal was never in the order data. It lived in a seven-decade-old regulation, a community's view of who a market is for, and a council that had already said no before.

Where does economics fit in?

Economics decides what is possible, culture decides what is acceptable and history decides what is remembered. People behave inside all three at once.

Consider Canadian travel to the United States. The obvious explanation for a drop is money: exchange rates, tariffs, prices. Leger's 2026 polling of Canadians who were less likely to travel south found that political tension was the most-cited reason (67%), ahead of tariffs and trade (61%) and safety concerns (nearly 60%). Economics mattered, but it arrived wrapped in identity. A pricing model would struggle to capture a reason like that.

What does a better method look like?

Not less data. More layers, in a sensible order.

  • Start with history. What has this place or group already decided about itself?
  • Add lived perception. What do people see, hear and feel that never makes it into a survey?
  • Then read the numbers, as a witness to be cross-examined rather than a judge to be obeyed.
  • Say how sure you are. A finding with a confidence level and a line on what would change your mind is more useful than a confident paragraph.
  • Allow "not enough signal." A partial answer, labelled partial, beats a confident answer built on thin evidence.

That is the discipline we are building into Ground Signal at The Whole Lot: history first, data third, humility throughout. Data is a witness, not a judge. It can tell you what happened. The verdict needs context.

Frequently asked questions

Why can't data alone explain human behaviour?

Data records what people did, not why. The same action can come from different causes, and those causes live in culture, history and economics that most datasets do not capture. Without that context, analysis tends to be accurate about the what and wrong about the why.

What is thick data?

Thick data is qualitative insight gathered through ethnography and similar methods: people's stories, emotions and models of their world. Ethnographer Tricia Wang popularised the term to describe what large quantitative datasets miss, and argues that businesses need both kinds of data.

What does WEIRD mean in behavioural research?

WEIRD stands for Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic. Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan argued in 2010 that behavioural science leaned heavily on such samples, which are often unrepresentative of humanity. A 2008 survey of top psychology journals found 96% of subjects came from Western industrialised countries.

What is Simpson's paradox?

Simpson's paradox is when a trend in combined data reverses or disappears once the data is split into groups. The 1973 Berkeley admissions case is the classic example: women's overall admission rate looked lower, but department by department the gap largely vanished.

title: How We're Building Ground Signal: A Business Intelligence System for Understanding What Data Misses
subtitle: Ground Signal is a business intelligence system being built by The Whole Lot in Bengaluru to explain why markets behave as they do. It reads a place's history, how people actually experience it and live public signals together, then says what is likely to happen next and how confident it is. It starts with history because behaviour is usually decided long before this week's data arrives.
author: Avani Jain
key_takeaways: Ground Signal explains. It does not just find documents or chart numbers.
Three rules: every claim traces to a source, every read carries a confidence level, and the system is allowed to answer "not enough signal."
It begins with history because the signal that matters often predates the dataset.
Today: a framework, a working prototype and sample reports. In build: source retrieval, grounding checks and a prediction record.
content:
What is Ground Signal?

Ground Signal is a business intelligence system built by The Whole Lot, a cultural intelligence and brand strategy company in Bengaluru, to explain why markets behave the way they do. It combines three kinds of reading: the history of a place or group, the lived experience of the people in it, and live public signals such as economic, cultural, discourse and policy data. The output is a read: what is happening, why now, what is likely next, and how sure we are.

The instinct predates the software. Before brands, the work was oral history and museum exhibitions: preserving what conventional records leave out. Ground Signal is that habit, structured. Observe, question, connect, understand, apply.

What problem is it trying to solve?

Dashboards are excellent at telling you what happened. General-purpose AI answers are excellent at sounding certain. Neither tells you why a market is behaving oddly, and neither reliably tells you when it is guessing.

The gap sits in the middle. Someone has to connect the economic number to the old law to the cultural habit, and say so plainly. That connecting is slow, expert work. We are trying to make it repeatable without making it shallow.

Why does it start with history?

Because the most important signal often predates the dataset. When Meghalaya's Khasi Hills Autonomous District Council refused Blinkit a trading licence in June 2026, the decision rested on a licensing system built on a 1954 regulation governing trading by non-tribals, and the council said it had already turned away comparable ventures, including Instamart.

A system that began with this week's order data would have noticed the problem on the day orders fell to zero. A system that began with local law and community history could have flagged it before launch. That is the whole case for history first.

How do we keep a system like this honest?

Four rules, treated as product requirements rather than good intentions.

  • Every claim traces to a source. The system should be unable to state a specific fact it cannot point to. Retrieval and reasoning are kept separate on purpose, with a check between them that removes any sentence it cannot support.
  • Every read carries a confidence level. High, medium or low, per claim, not one comforting badge on the whole report. When sources disagree, the disagreement is shown, not smoothed over.
  • The system may say "not enough signal." A partial answer, labelled partial, beats a confident answer built on thin evidence.
  • Certain disclaimers are inserted by code, not by the model. The line saying a read explains a tendency and not an individual cannot be forgotten, because nobody has to remember it.

We tested the discipline on Dwarka, the submerged city of the Mahabharata. The useful finding was not a verdict on whether it existed. Physical excavations did happen, and the archaeologist who led them published a date range of roughly 1500 to 1700 BCE. The dates circulating online today are far older and contradict one another. What came out was a confidence-tiered account of what the evidence supports, where it stops, and how far the public story has run ahead of it. That is what a good output looks like: less thrilling than a verdict, and far more useful.

There is also a line we chose not to cross. Ground Signal is not pointed at living people. Online sleuthing has wrongly named innocent individuals before, and a tool that sounds sourced and organised makes that mistake more convincing, not less.

What exists today, and what is still being built?

Component Status What it means
Framework: history, lived experience, live signals Built The method and its structure are defined
Interactive prototype Built City profiles for 29 cities across six regions, with a live read generator
Sample reports Built Worked reads on real situations, including quick commerce in India, cross-border tourism and Dwarka
Source retrieval and evidence store In build Each claim tied to a stored, dated source
Grounding check and abstention In build Unsupported sentences removed; thin evidence returns a partial read
Prediction record In build Forecasts logged with dates, then graded later, including the wrong ones
Client data connections Planned Ad platforms and analytics, read-only

The prototype reasons from context we give it, not yet from retrieved sources. That is exactly the gap the build closes.

How will we know it works?

A system that explains things should be graded on what it predicts. The plan is a prediction record: every "what happens next" claim logged with a date and a check-back window, then marked right, wrong or partly right. Early outputs get human review before anything is automated. We also plan to run the method on cases with a checkable answer, to see whether it rediscovers what is already known.

Who is it for?

Anyone making a decision that depends on understanding people rather than counting them: strategists, founders, investors, institutions. The same market reads differently depending on who is asking and why, so the system asks that first. A customer who wants to understand a delivery fee and a founder scoping a competitor need different answers from the same evidence.

The point is not more data. It is connecting the data people already have in a way no one has bothered to, and being honest about how sure we are.

Frequently asked questions

What is Ground Signal?

Ground Signal is a business intelligence system being built by The Whole Lot, a Bengaluru-based cultural intelligence and brand strategy company. It reads a place's history, the lived experience of its people and live public signals together to explain market behaviour, forecast what is likely next and state how confident it is.

How is Ground Signal different from a dashboard or a general AI chatbot?

A dashboard reports what happened, and a general chatbot answers from what it has learned. Ground Signal is designed to answer from retrieved, dated sources it can show, to carry a confidence level on each claim, and to decline when evidence is thin. It starts from history rather than this week's data.

Is Ground Signal available now?

Not as a self-serve product yet. A working prototype and sample reports exist, and the retrieval, grounding and prediction-tracking layers are in build. For a sample read on a specific market or brand question, get in touch with The Whole Lot.

Why does Ground Signal start with history?

Because behaviour is often shaped by decisions made long before today's data: old regulations, trade patterns, community norms. The 2026 Blinkit licensing refusal in Meghalaya rested on a 1954 regulation, a signal no recent dataset would have shown until orders stopped.

title: Is SEO Dead in 2026? What SEO, AEO and GEO Actually Mean for Brands
subtitle: No, SEO is not dead in 2026, but it is no longer the whole game. SEO earns a ranked link. AEO (Answer Engine Optimization) earns the answer or snippet itself. GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) earns a citation inside an AI-generated response. The three overlap, and strong SEO foundations still help AI systems find and trust a page.
author: Avani Jain
key_takeaways: SEO is not dying, but the click it used to earn is getting rarer. In Pew's study, searches with an AI summary got link clicks 8% of the time against 15% without.
AEO and GEO extend SEO rather than replace it. One Forrester analyst called the differences significant but not fundamental.

What gets cited is clear, extractable, well-supported content. The original GEO research found that citations, quotations and statistics lifted visibility by up to 40%, while keyword stuffing did little.
The evidence base is thin and much of the advice comes from vendors. Measure your own results.
content:
What do SEO, AEO and GEO actually mean?

SEO AEO GEO
Full name Search Engine Optimization Answer Engine Optimization Generative Engine Optimization
Optimises for A ranked link on a results page Being the direct answer: snippets, voice results, AI answer boxes Being cited inside an AI-written response (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude)
Success looks like Position and clicks Selection as the answer Citations and brand mentions
Core levers Relevance, authority, speed, links Question headings, short direct answers, FAQs, structured data Original statistics, attributed quotations, citations, clear claims

A caution: the vocabulary is not settled. Wikipedia's entry on GEO notes that as of early 2026 no consensus definition separated these terms in the academic literature, and that practitioners often use them interchangeably. Some vendors treat AEO as the umbrella, others treat GEO as the broader discipline. The academic term GEO comes from a paper presented at the ACM SIGKDD conference in 2024 by researchers from Princeton, Georgia Tech, the Allen Institute for AI and IIT Delhi.

Forrester analyst Nikhil Lai has argued that AEO and its cousins are "significantly, but not fundamentally" different from SEO, and suggested that advocates of the new acronyms tend to exaggerate the gap to carve out a market for themselves. Worth keeping in mind, including when reading this article.

What does the 2026 evidence say about search traffic?

The sharpest data is still Pew Research Center's study of 900 US adults, using browsing data from March 2025. When a Google AI Overview appeared, users clicked a traditional result link 8% of the time, against 15% when it did not. Only 1% clicked a source cited inside the summary. Sessions ended more often, 26% against 16%, which suggests the summary may simply be working for the searcher. Google disputed the study's methodology. Ahrefs separately reported that AI Overviews cut click-through on the top result by 34.5%.

Gartner forecast in 2024 that traditional search engine volume would fall 25% by 2026, with AI chatbots taking the share. Search Engine Journal argued at the time that the forecast assumed search engines would stand still. That year is now. We did not find an independent measurement confirming a 25% drop, which is not the same as showing it has not happened.

For scale, one AEO agency cites Semrush data from 2025 putting ChatGPT at about 700 million weekly users and Google AI Overviews at about 2 billion monthly users. Treat vendor-cited figures as indicative.

Is trust in AI answers keeping pace with usage?

Not yet. Fractl's Q2 2026 survey of 1,008 consumers found AI search use rising while perceived helpfulness fell: the share saying AI search was more helpful dropped from 82% to 54% in a year, and the share calling it less helpful rose from 3% to 17%. In the same survey, 27% of marketers said their brand had been inaccurately described in an AI-generated answer, and 14% said an AI inaccuracy had affected a real customer relationship, sale or PR situation.

People use AI answers and do not fully trust them. That makes the sources an AI cites a trust signal in themselves. Being cited is borrowed credibility. Being described wrongly is lost credibility.

What actually gets a brand cited?

The one peer-reviewed study is the GEO paper by Aggarwal and colleagues, presented at KDD 2024. Across a benchmark of roughly 10,000 queries, adding citations, quotations from relevant sources and statistics improved visibility in generative responses by up to 40%, and by up to 37% on Perplexity, a live commercial engine. Keyword stuffing, the classic SEO shortcut, offered little to no improvement.

Practitioner consensus, which is less rigorous, adds answer-first structure, question-style headings, concise answers directly under each heading, structured FAQs and schema markup. One summary puts it plainly: answer engines pick sources that are easy to extract, clearly worded and well supported.

Notice what that list rewards: specificity, attribution and clarity. It is an old editorial virtue wearing a new acronym.

So is SEO dead? What changes and what does not

What is dying is the strategy of publishing thin pages to catch clicks. What is not dying is the foundation: crawlable, fast, authoritative pages that answer real questions. Bing's own documentation says SEO fundamentals support eligibility for AI-generated experiences. SEO is the fuel. AEO and GEO decide whether the page becomes the answer.

What should brands do in 2026?

  • Keep the foundations. Crawlable, fast, authoritative pages. Everything else sits on top.
  • Write answer-first. Open every page with a direct answer to its own question, then earn the reader's time with depth. You may have noticed where this article started.
  • Structure for extraction. Question-style headings, short definitions, tables where comparison helps, an FAQ section, and structured data such as Article and FAQ schema.
  • Publish what only you can. Original data, first-hand observation, named experts. Statistics and attributed quotations are what the GEO research found AI systems cite.
  • Measure citations, not just rankings. Track whether AI answers mention you, for which questions, and what they say. Sample the questions your customers ask in each major engine every month.
  • Audit how AI describes you. More than a quarter of marketers in Fractl's survey said their brand had been described inaccurately. Fix the source pages those answers draw on.
  • Keep a human accountable. A named author, a date and a point of view are signals for readers and for machines alike.

How much of this advice should you trust?

Treat it as a working hypothesis. Much of the AEO and GEO advice online is published by vendors who sell AEO and GEO services. The one peer-reviewed study dates from 2024 and tested simulated engines plus one commercial one. Test on your own pages, and expect the advice to date quickly.

SEO is not dead. It got a roommate, and the roommate answers questions faster than you do. The brands that win will be the ones worth quoting.

Frequently asked questions

Is SEO dead in 2026?

No. SEO is changing, not disappearing. AI answers reduce clicks on traditional links (Pew found 8% against 15%), but strong SEO fundamentals still help search and AI systems find and trust pages. The shift is from earning rankings alone to earning rankings, answers and citations.

What is the difference between SEO, AEO and GEO?

SEO optimises for ranked links, AEO for direct answers such as snippets and AI answer boxes, and GEO for citations inside AI-generated responses. Definitions vary by source, and most practitioners treat them as overlapping layers of one visibility strategy.

How do I get cited by ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity?

Publish clear, well-sourced, answer-first content with specific statistics, attributed quotations and structured data. In the 2024 GEO study, adding citations, quotations and statistics improved visibility by up to 40%, while keyword stuffing did little. Results vary by engine, so test your own pages.

What is Generative Engine Optimization?

Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) is the practice of structuring content and managing online presence so AI systems cite and represent it accurately in generated answers. The term was formalised in a peer-reviewed paper presented at ACM SIGKDD 2024.

Do I need to do AEO and GEO separately from SEO?

Not as separate programmes. They share the same foundations: clear, authoritative, well-structured content. Add answer-first structure, FAQs and citations on top of sound SEO, then measure rankings, answer inclusion and AI citations side by side.
